title: Paying Extra for A2 Ghee? Cardiologist Says the Label Is a Fad
excerpt: Dr. Darshan Banker and the IFBA's Deepak Jolly say the A1/A2 protein distinction is irrelevant in ghee, which is 99.9% fat — portion size and verified purity matter far more.
body:
• A cardiologist and a food-industry chief say the "A2" label on ghee is essentially a marketing device: since ghee is 99.9% fat, the A1/A2 protein distinction that applies to milk is irrelevant in clarified butter.
  • Dr. Darshan Banker, interventional cardiologist at Bankers Heart Institute in Vadodara, calls premium A2 ghee "just a fad" and says what matters is how much saturated fat you consume, not which label is on the jar.
  • The scepticism cuts against a boom: the A2 and organic ghee sub-segment is growing at over 22% a year, nearly three times the pace of the overall category, per IMARC Group.
  • Doctors' real checklist: portion control (under a teaspoon a day for those with normal cholesterol), and verification of FSSAI licensing and purity — adulteration, not the A2 label, is the bigger consumer risk.

You are paying three to four times the price of regular ghee because the jar says "A2." According to one cardiologist and the head of a national food-industry body, that label is telling you almost nothing about your heart.

"The A1 and A2 claims refer to the type of protein found in milk," said Deepak Jolly, chairperson of the Indian Food and Beverage Association. "Since ghee consists of 99.9% fat, the reference A1 ghee and A2 ghee are mere marketing gimmicks."

The cardiologist's case

Dr. Darshan Banker, an interventional cardiologist at Bankers Heart Institute in Vadodara, made the same point in clinical terms. The A1/A2 distinction is about beta-casein protein in milk, he explained — but clarification strips protein out. "When you process and make ghee out of it, there is no protein left. There is no casein left in the ghee, so it is irrelevant. According to me, whether it is A2 ghee or A1 ghee, it is just a fad."

His prescription has nothing to do with labels: "American College of Cardiology guidelines say saturated fat consumption as less as possible is beneficial... moderation remains the ultimate rule for your arteries — no matter what the label says."

What to check instead

If the A2 stamp isn't the health signal, what is? Two things, say the experts. First, quantity. Dr. Jyoti Kusnur, consultant in interventional cardiology at Manipal Hospital in Goa, told Mint that for people with normal cholesterol and no heart disease, "less than a teaspoon a day is generally the amount commensurate with" causing no harm — and that excess saturated fat over time raises LDL cholesterol regardless of the jar's claims.

Second, purity. The food regulator FSSAI advises consumers to verify the FSSAI licence number, labelling information and manufacturer details, check packaging integrity, and be wary of unusually low prices — a real concern after enforcement drives seized around 6,500 litres of suspected adulterated ghee in Delhi and Haryana in June 2026. Adulteration, not the A1/A2 debate, is where most consumers' money is actually at risk.

The boom the sceptics are bucking

The pushback lands in the middle of a premiumisation wave. India's A2 and organic ghee sub-segment is expanding at over 22 per cent annually between 2025 and 2033 — nearly three times the overall category's growth, per IMARC Group data reported by The Hindu BusinessLine. A PwC 2025 consumer survey found 84 per cent of Indian respondents actively seeking safer, healthier food and 73 per cent willing to pay more for sustainably produced food. That is the market paying for provenance — and the premium label is exactly what sceptics say is being oversold.

"Since ghee consists of 99.9% fat, the reference A1 ghee and A2 ghee are mere marketing gimmicks."

— Deepak Jolly, chairperson, Indian Food and Beverage Association

Not every cardiologist agrees

The medical community is not unanimous. Dr. Alok Chopra, a Delhi cardiologist with 40 years of experience, has called A2 ghee "pure fuel for the body and brain" and recommends 1–2 teaspoons per meal, chosen as high-quality, preferably A2, within a balanced diet. The honest state of the science: current research does not prove ghee is a miracle food for the heart, and experts across the spectrum agree that moderation is what moves the needle.

Diaspora angle

NRIs are squarely in the premium market — A2 ghee jars in US Indian grocery stores routinely sell at double or triple the price of regular ghee, marketed on health claims imported from Indian advertising. The advice translates directly: buy the ghee whose purity you can verify, watch the portion, and don't pay a health premium for a protein distinction that disappears in clarification.

What's next

Neither the FSSAI nor any regulator currently defines what qualifies as "A2 ghee," which means the label is functionally unverifiable for most consumers — anyone can print it without sourcing from verified A2 breeds. Until standards exist, the safest check remains the boring one: licence number, seal, manufacturer — and the spoon in your hand.
